newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-RBA SAYS IT HAS NO AUSTRALIAN GROWTH TARGET.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-RBA SAYS IT HAS NO AUSTRALIAN GROWTH TARGET.

text.p: Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) Governor Ian Macfarlane said on Tuesday the bank did not have a growth ceiling and the economy could grow 4.5 percent or more over the next few years without sparking inflation.

Speaking to a meeting of the Australian Institute of Company Directors, Macfarlane also said current monetary policy was not placing any constraints on growth and was maximising the chances for a long recovery.
"We do not have a growth target, beyond which the brakes automatically go on," Macfarlane said.

He said he did not know where a perceived annual growth ceiling of 3.5 percent had come from. The misconception may have arisen as it was a figure he had once quoted, for comparison purposes only, as the average growth rate of the economy over the last six years, he said.

"We have an inflation target, appropriately and flexibly defined, which tells us to tighten when our forecast of inflation has it exceeding the target for any sustained period of time, and to ease when the forecast has inflation sustainably below target," Macfarlane said.
As such, growth did not necessarily trigger a policy response, he said.

The RBA targets the underlying rate of inflation -- which strips out the more volatile elements of the consumer price index -- aiming to keep it to an average of between two and three percent over a run of years.
In the year to June underlying inflation was 1.7 percent, the lowest annual rate on record.
"This approach (to inflation) is not, as some might think, anti-growth," Macfarlane said.
"It is, in fact, pro-growth by favouring forward looking management of the business cycle, which will help in achieving a stable platform for long-run growth," he said.
Sustained periods of strong growth had always occured with low inflation, he said.
Apart from laying the platform for prolonging the current six-year economic expansion, current policy settings were conducive to expected stronger growth in 1997, he said.

"At the moment I do not see that monetary policy is placing any contraint on growth," Macfarlane said, saying the target made sure monetary policy was eased when the inflation forecast is below the target average.

"The main test of what is sustainable on the growth front is the inflation test: is the rate of growth compatible with achieving the two to three percent (inflation) average, looking forward as best we can over a year or two?," he said.
Given a favourable outlook for inflation, the economy was likely to post above average growth in coming years after a period of below average growth in 1996, he said.

"With inflation tamed, and with some slack available, we should be quite capable of growing by 3.5 percent, four percent, 4.5 percent -- or possibly even faster -- over the next couple of years without any significant detrimental effect on inflation," he said.
Macfarlane said these growth rates were not targets but were illustrative of the growth that might be reasonably expected after a period of slow growth such as in 1996.

"People are disappointed that more progress has not yet been made on reducing unemployment, but we have made some, and further real progress will be made if we can sustain a long running expansion," he said.

"...I think our current monetary policy framework is serving us well in this regard, by requiring us to take a medium-term view in our policy deliberations and maximising the chances for a long recovery," he said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
